bull_case: Adobe can use its installed base, proprietary workflow data and commercial-safety positioning to absorb AI disruption.
bear_case: If creation shifts to prompt-native platforms that bypass Adobe apps, AI becomes a moat reducer rather than extender.
thesis: Adobe is an incumbent responding effectively to generative AI rather than a pure disruptive entrant. Firefly, Acrobat agents and Experience Cloud AI can expand the market, but open/model-native tools can also commoditize portions of Adobe's workflow.

evidence.claim: AI-first ARR grew >150% y/y in Q3.
Adobe reported >1B MAU across creativity and productivity.

counterevidence: AI lowers content-creation barriers and could shift value from application vendors toward models, distribution layers or new agentic workflows.
unknowns: Long-run AI monetization per user, Firefly inference economics, and how much AI-first ARR is incremental versus bundled/reclassified ARR.
falsifiers: If ARR growth falls to low single digits while AI usage rises, or owner FCF/share stops compounding despite buybacks, the moat/compounder thesis is downgraded.
next_checks: Q4/FY2026 ARR, AI-first ARR, OCF, SBC, repurchases, share count and Digital Media/Experience growth

subscores.rationale: Adobe is adapting to AI rather than creating a wholly new 10x cost curve; Firefly lowers creation costs but model competition is intense.
AI-first ARR +150% and >1B MAU show rapid adoption, but monetization depth is still emerging.
Creative, document and customer-experience workflows provide multiple AI monetization surfaces.

uncertainties.rationale: AI monetization and competitive workflow migration remain the central uncertainty.
